narrative:
The model predicts you have a 13% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your reason for choosing this school, your history of past failures, and your desire to pursue higher education. Surprisingly, the top influence was your reason for choosing the school: you selected it because it was close to home. Among students who passed, only 24% chose the school for this reason, while most chose it for the course itself or its reputation. This choice pushed the prediction toward failing.

Your record of zero past class failures was the second most important factor. This actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing, since having no previous failures is typical of students who succeed.

Wanting to continue to higher education was the third strongest influence. Like every student who passed, you have this ambition, which also nudged the outcome toward passing.

Even though two of the top three factors supported success, the impact of choosing the school mainly for location outweighed them, tipping the model toward a risk of failure.

To improve, think carefully about your study habits and school engagement. Since you study only 2–5 hours per week, have no extra support, and miss more classes than the average successful student (6 days versus 3.8), focusing on consistent attendance, seeking extra help, and using your ambition for higher education as daily motivation could make a real difference.
